newsitem.title: TURKEY: Turkmen leader promises citizens quick prosperity.
newsitem.headline: Turkmen leader promises citizens quick prosperity.

text.p: Turkmen President Saparmurat Niyazov, focus of a growing personality cult in his Central Asian republic, has told his impoverished countrymen that living standards will grow three-fold over the next five years.

"Every citizen of Turkmenistan, irrespective of his nationality, must find in his motherland happiness and prosperity," newpapers quoted Niyazov as saying over the weekend, which marked the fifth anniversary of his election.

Niyazov -- the former Soviet republic's top Communist party leader -- was elected president in a referendum on June 21, 1992. Officials said 99.5 percent of the voters chose Niyazov, the single candidate on the list.

Niyazov, also known as Turkmenbashi or "head of the Turkmens", ordered a new referendum in January 1994 to extend his presidency until 2002. Official propaganda said the proposal was backed by 99.9 percent of those who voted.
But Niyazov's promises of a better life for his resource-rich but desperately impoverished desert nation of some four million people seem unlikely to be realised very fast.

Salaries average a mere $33 a month and Niyazov's plan to achieve self-sufficiency in grain collapsed last year, bringing in its wake bread shortages and expensive grain imports that cost the state $800 million.

The official Turkmen Press news agency quoted Niyazov as telling economy chiefs at the weekend that Turkmenistan hoped to gather a total grain harvest of 1.2 million tonnes this year and achieve an annual production of 2.0 million tonnes by 2000. Last year saw a disastrous harvest of 430,000 tonnes.
"Saparmurat Turkmenbashi has cordially thanked those present for congratulations in his address, stressing that he views this solemn date as an event of national importance," the agency said.
Portraits of the leader gaze down on passers-by from virtually every street corner in the capital and many schools, towns and military units bear his name.
In April Niyazov presented to the nation his own economic programme "1,000 days" which aims to bring a giant leap in the country's economic development.
"Conscientious work during the forthcoming 1,000 days is the source of a 1,000-year prosperity," the programme said in its preamble.
In line with the programme, Turkmenistan's output of cotton is supposed to jump to 1.2 million tonnes and to 2.0 million tonnes from last year's 480,000 tonnes.
"I do not believe this and other promises. My relatives in the cotton-growing region of Tashauz have no money to buy even cottonseed oil," Rustam, a scientist in his 70s, told Reuters in Ashgabat.

The production of natural gas -- Turkmenistan's main natural asset -- should leap to 284 billion cubic metres in 2000 from last year's 35.2 billion, and of crude oil to 10 million tonnes from four million tonnes last year.
Niyazov, who tolerates little opposition in his country, is fiercely proud of Turkmenistan's official status of neutrality.

This has encouraged avid discussion in the local press of plans to build in central Ashgabat an Arch of Neutrality 70 metres (210 feet) long, with a 12 metre (36 foot) revolving statue of Niyazov on top of it.
